To register to vote in North Carolina, a voter must have lived in the county they are registering in for at least 30 days before Election Day. Voters who moved more recently are not eligible to vote in that particular county, but may be able to vote at their previous residence.  However, if a voter moved within the same county more than 30 days before an election but did not update their address with the board of elections, they may vote as normal. Early voting in NC in 2026. Everything you need to know.

by Sarah Michels, Carolina Public Press
October 19, 2026

North Carolinians began to vote early Thursday, Oct. 15. By the end of the first weekend, 485,531 people had voted early in the 2026 general election. Including absentee voters, 6.67% of North Carolina registered voters have already voted. 

There’s still a lot of time for voters who haven’t made it to the polls yet. Early voting will run through 3 p.m., Saturday, Oct. 31. 

When and where can I vote early? 

Voting hours and locations vary across counties, based on the decisions of county election boards. 

[Subscribe for FREE to Carolina Public Press’ Daily, Weekend and Election 2026 newsletters.]

Every county must conduct early voting on weekdays between Thursday, Oct. 15, and Friday, Oct. 30 from 8 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. They are also required by law to hold early voting on the final Saturday before Election Day from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. This year, the final day of early voting lands on Halloween. 

However, county election boards decide whether they have early voting on the first two weekends of the early voting period. They also may differ on the hours polls are open. Voters can figure out exactly when and where they can vote at the State Board of Elections website or their county election board website. 

This cycle, 17 out of 100 counties are having early voting on at least one Sunday, less than half of the 40 counties who did so in the 2022 midterm election. 

Thanks to a 2024 law shifting election appointment power from the governor to the state auditor, county election board majorities flipped from Democratic to Republican in mid-2025. Many of the new Republican majorities led their counties to cut Sunday early voting. However, a majority of counties still offer at least one day of Saturday early voting in the first two weekends of the early voting period. 

Early voting locations may have changed since the last time voters went to the polls, too. Unlike on Election Day, voters may choose any early voting location in their county to cast their ballot. They may find the closest polling place at the State Board’s website. 

On Election Day, voters must vote at their specified precinct, which they can find on their voter file. 

What do I need to bring to early voting?

Under North Carolina law, all voters must provide a valid form of photo identification to vote. 

Acceptable voter ID includes North Carolina driver’s licenses, non-driver IDs from the Division of Motor Vehicles, US passports, approved student and public employee IDs, US government-issued military or veterans ID cards, tribal enrollment cards and other ID cards including photos issued by a US government agency or North Carolina public assistance program. 

If voters are new to North Carolina, and registered to vote within 90 days of the election, they may use out-of-state drivers license or non-driver ID. 

Registered voters lacking a photo ID may get a free one from their county election boards by visiting the offices during business hours before early voting ends and providing their names, birthdays and the last four digits of their Social Security numbers. County election officials will take their photos. Depending on the county, the photo ID may be available immediately or need to be mailed. 

How do I find out who is on my ballot? 

Voters can find sample ballots online by using the State Board of Election’s voter search tool. If voters want to practice filling it out or print out a completed sample ballot, they can do so by using option 4 on the absentee ballot portal. 

At polling places, electioneers may hand out sample ballots to voters based on their party affiliations. Those are only suggestions; voters do not have to listen to anybody at the polling location except for election officials. 

How can I avoid early voting lines?

Many county election boards have online wait estimates on their websites. 

Generally, most early voters go the first couple of days, the last couple of days and on weekends. Voters’ best shot at avoiding a crowd is casting a ballot on a weekday. 

Do I have to sign up to vote early?

No, voters do not have to sign up or take any extra steps to vote early. All they must do is show up to a polling location in their county with a valid form of voter ID. 

Even North Carolinians who missed the voter registration deadline can vote early. During early voting hours, North Carolina election officials offer same-day registration, which allows people to register to vote and cast their ballot at the same time. Same-day registrants also have to show proof that they live in the county. They can use a North Carolina driver’s license, a government or school-issued photo identification with their current residential address, or a utility bill, paycheck, bank statement or other government document with their current name and address. 

What if I recently moved and my address is not up to date?

To register to vote in North Carolina, a voter must have lived in the county they are registering in for at least 30 days before Election Day. Voters who moved more recently are not eligible to vote in that particular county, but may be able to vote at their previous residence. 

However, if a voter moved within the same county more than 30 days before an election but did not update their address with the board of elections, they may vote as normal. Voters with this kind of unreported move should tell election officials their new address so they can receive the correct ballot.

What if I need help voting? 

Voters with physical limitations may use curbside voting. These voters sign a statement stating that they cannot enter the polling place without help due to their age or physical disability. Election officials will then guide them through the voting process from their cars. 

Voters may ask for assistance voting from a spouse, sibling, parent, child, grandparent, grandchild or in-law. Voters who have a physical disability, are blind or are illiterate may ask for anyone’s help, besides their employer. The chief judge must approve this assistance and determine that it is appropriate. 

Precinct officials will keep a record of anyone who assists a voter. 

Can I use my phone when voting?

Voters may use their phones in limited ways while early voting. They can consult them as a research guide if needed to complete their ballot, but they cannot take photos or video inside the polling place for privacy reasons. 

So called “ballot selfies” are not permitted, although they have been the subject of a lawsuit. 

Voters also may not use their phone to communicate with anyone while voting. 

What if I have a problem while voting?

Voters who have issues at the polling place have several options. 

First, they can talk to an election official about their problem — either the chief judge on site or the county election director. The State Board of Elections also may be able to help; its phone number is (919) 814-0700. 

Voters may also see signs at their polling place with numbers of voter hotlines. Several nonpartisan groups set up these hotlines ahead of elections for voters. 

These include 888-OUR-VOTE (888-687-8683) and 888-Ve-Y-VOTA (888-839-8682) for Spanish speakers. 

Voters are always allowed to vote provisionally, no matter the circumstance. Election officials should provide one if requested. 

I was told to vote a provisional ballot? What does that mean? 

Voters must vote provisional ballots when election officials cannot find them on the list of registered voters eligible to vote at that polling location, or there is another issue.

When a person votes provisionally, they make a written affirmation that they are an eligible, registered voter in that jurisdiction and then fill out a ballot. Those ballots will later be reviewed by the county elections board to determine whether the ballot may count fully, partially or not at all. 

Several situations could lead to a voter having to vote provisionally. 

Voters who forget their photo ID or are missing one may vote provisionally. They will be asked to either come back later to the county election board with their voter ID or fill out a photo ID exception form explaining why they do not have one. 

A voter may appear at the wrong polling location on Election Day, meaning that they are only eligible to vote in some of the races on their ballot. During early voting, this is less of an issue since voters may go to any polling location in their county. 

Voters on the Registration Repair Project list will be asked to vote a provisional ballot because their voter record lacks a required identification number — either the last four digits of their Social Security number or their driver’s license number. If election officials can validate the updated information, that voter’s ballot will count. 

Provisional voters will receive information about how to check whether their vote was counted. 

What happens to my ballot after I cast it? How do I know early voting is secure? 

After the end of early voting each day, the ballot box or other system containing completed early voting ballots will be secured according to a State Board of Elections approved plan. 

Early votes will not be counted until after polls close on Election Day. 

Can anyone see how I voted? 

The act of voting is public record. When a voter casts a ballot, their method of voting will be recorded on their public voter file. 

However, nobody will see the specific selections a voter made. 

One note: a poll worker may write on a voter’s ballot. That does not invalidate it, and may be necessary for various reasons. 

I’ve heard that armed law enforcement officers might be at the polls. Is that true? Is that allowed? 

US Department of Homeland Security figures said they are not planning to send Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers to the polls this election cycle, at least not in a systemic way. 

However, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said while ICE isn’t meant to patrol polling places, they may be there “to enforce specific threats.”

“The only reason why we would be at polling places if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving on someone that we have been actively tracking down,” he said in September. 

In April, NC State Board of Election Democrats asked to give county election officials more guidance on how to handle ICE or other federal law enforcement showing up to the polls, particularly if they ask to seize ballots or disrupt order. 

Board Republicans declined to issue that guidance. Federal and state law was enough, they said. 

“We have to be careful of preparing verging on the edge of fearmongering,” Republican board chair Francis De Luca said. 

Under federal law, military officials cannot bring, keep or control any troops or armed military at voting sites “unless such force be necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.” It’s also illegal to “intimidate, threaten, coerce or attempt to intimidate, threaten or coerce” a voter to influence how or whether they vote. 

State law allows chief judges to “enforce peace and good order” at polling places. As part of that responsibility, they are required to “prevent and stop improper practices and attempts to obstruct, intimidate, or interfere with any person in registering or voting” and “prevent riots, violence, tumult, or disorder.” 

They may call law enforcement to help them enforce the law, and order the arrest of people violating the law. 

I got a letter in the mail telling me that I might not be a citizen based on the SAVE database. Can I vote? 

The State Board of Elections recently sent letters to 1,392 registered voters informing them that they were identified as potential noncitizens through the federal Systemic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) system. 

These voters are not automatically removed from the voter rolls, since the SAVE system is known to include outdated and missing information. 

If voters are US citizens eligible to vote, they can still vote. If they are not citizens — including legal residents — they should not vote, even if allowed. These voters may get into trouble after the election if election boards find out that they illegally voted.
